The Brown comber (Serranus hepatus) is a small serranid fish inhabiting the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent Atlantic waters, and its life-history strategy reflects the constraints of a relatively short-lived, iteroparous lifestyle. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a total length of 7.8 cm [Lp = 7.8 cm] at the onset of gonad maturation, a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 6 grams [Wwp = approximately 6 grams]. This reproductive milestone is reached early in the lifespan, allowing the species to capitalize on favourable environmental conditions within its first year of growth. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], with the corresponding maximum adult body mass reaching 209 grams [Wwi = 209 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions on sampled individuals. Such asymptotic measurements are consistent with a species that dedicates a substantial portion of its somatic growth to early reproduction, a pattern common among small-bodied marine teleosts subject to moderate predation pressure.

Under local thermal regimes averaging 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the population mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) is 5% [GSI = 5%]. This value aligns closely with estimates for other iteroparous serranids of comparable body size. The small size of the neonates, with a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams], suggests that the species produces numerous, highly fecund eggs that undergo a pelagic larval phase. The yolk-sac larva that emerges from the demersal egg relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical bottleneck in the early life history of most marine finfish.

The maximum lifespan of the Brown comber of 11 years [am = 11 years] has been estimated from scale and otolith readings taken from wild-caught specimens, with the standard aquarium temperature maintained at 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C] during holding periods for validation studies. This longevity is relatively modest compared to larger groupers in the Serranidae family, though it is considerable for a fish of such small asymptotic dimensions. The combination of a 25 cm [Li = 25 cm] ultimate length and an 11-year lifespan implies a relatively slow annual growth increment after sexual maturity, with individuals prioritizing physiological upkeep over rapid somatic expansion. Natural mortality in older age classes is primarily driven by predation from piscivorous fishes and cephalopods, as well as senescence-related physiological deterioration.

Puberty, defined by the first onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, occurs when the fish reaches a total length of 7.8 cm [Lp = 7.8 cm], a threshold that may be attained within the first year of benthic juvenile life. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 6 grams [Wwp = 6 grams] marks the transition from an immature sub-adult to a reproductively active adult capable of participating in spawning aggregations. This early maturation strategy is ecologically advantageous in variable environments, allowing Serranus hepatus to produce offspring before the risk of mortality becomes too high. Histological examination confirms that the gonadosomatic index remains close to 5% [GSI = 5%] during the peak spawning months at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C].

The pelagic larval phase of Serranus hepatus begins with the emergence of a yolk-sac larva that weighs only 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams] at hatching, a minimal initial mass that imposes a strong selective pressure for rapid yolk absorption and the commencement of exogenous feeding. After settlement, the juvenile fish grow toward the ultimate total length of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], with the asymptotic wet weight of 209 grams [Wwi = 209 grams] typically approached by older individuals. The observed lifespan of 4015 days [am = 4015 days] under field conditions at a mean water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C] suggests that the species maintains a stable metabolic rate well into its later years. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that the life-history parameters of Serranus hepatus are representative of a temperate, reef-associated serranid with a balanced trade-off between current reproduction and future survival.
